---
title: "Fit Objects"
---

Everything on this site that starts with a fitted model starts with the object
`bgm()` or `bgmCompare()` returned. This page documents that object: the class
it belongs to, the fields it holds, which of them cost nothing and which are
computed on demand, and the rules that govern reading them.

Four files define it. `R/class_s7.R` declares the two S7 classes and the
converters that build them. `R/fit_accessors.R` holds the internal readers the
rest of the package uses. `R/methods_bgms.R` and `R/methods_bgmcompare.R` hold
the user-facing methods, including the `$` and `[[` methods that keep the
object usable as if it were still a list.

For what to do with the object, see [Model Output](../guide/mcmc-output.qmd) in
the Guide and the [Methods reference](../reference/methods.qmd).

## Two classes

`bgm()` returns an object of class `bgms`; `bgmCompare()` returns one of class
`bgmCompare`. Both are S7 classes with `package = NULL`, which means they carry
the bare class names `"bgms"` and `"bgmCompare"` alongside `"S7_object"`, so
existing S3 dispatch on those names keeps working. Every user-facing method in
the package is registered as an S3 method against those names.

The two classes hold different parameter fields, because the models
parameterize differently. A `bgms` fit stores main effects and pairwise
associations directly. A `bgmCompare` fit stores a baseline and a set of
contrasts, and stores them separately: `posterior_mean_main_baseline`,
`posterior_mean_pairwise_baseline`, `posterior_mean_main_differences`, and
`posterior_mean_pairwise_differences`. Turning those into one group's
parameters is a computation, not a lookup, and is what
[`extract_group_params()`](../reference/extractors.qmd#extract_group_params)
does.

## How the object is built

The object is assembled as an ordinary named list first and converted at the
very end. `build_output()` dispatches on the model type to
`build_output_bgm()` (which serves both the GGM and the ordinal MRF),
`build_output_mixed_mrf()`, or `build_output_compare()`. Each builder fills a
plain list, sets its class to `"bgms"` or `"bgmCompare"`, and finishes by
calling `s3_list_to_bgms()` or `s3_list_to_bgmCompare()`, which copies each
element into the matching S7 property.

There is one escape hatch. `needs_easybgm_s3_compat()` returns the plain list
uncoverted when the `easybgm` namespace is loaded at a version below 0.5.0,
with a warning naming the version. A fit made that way is a list, not an S7
object, which is why every internal reader in the package handles both forms.

The conversion also records `names(results)` into the `.field_names` property.
That single line is the whole `names()` contract, described below.

## What the object stores

### Always present

`arguments` is the settings record: dimensions, priors, sampler configuration,
variable metadata, the package version that produced the fit, and the recode
maps. It is built by `build_arguments()` (see
[R Scaffolding](r-scaffolding.qmd#the-arguments-record)) and read by almost
everything downstream. `raw_samples` holds the per-chain draw matrices.
`cache` is an environment, discussed below.

`raw_samples` is assembled by `build_raw_samples_list()` and always carries
`main`, `pairwise`, `nchains`, `niter`, and a `parameter_names` list. Under
edge selection it additionally carries `indicator`, plus the
Rao-Blackwellized inclusion draws `rb_inclusion` and the odds accumulators
`rb_counts` described under
[GGM Internals](ggm-internals.qmd#rao-blackwellized-inclusion-draws). Under a
stochastic block prior it also carries `allocations`.

### Posterior means

The `posterior_mean_*` fields are computed during construction, because they
are only column means over the pooled draws. They are set once and never
recomputed. Which ones exist depends on the model: a GGM fit has no main
effects and therefore a `NULL` `posterior_mean_main`, but it does have
`posterior_mean_residual_variance`; an ordinal fit is the other way around.
Edge selection adds `posterior_mean_indicator`, and a stochastic block prior
adds the co-clustering matrix, the mean and modal allocations, and the
posterior distribution over the number of blocks.

### Sampler diagnostics

`nuts_diag`, `am_diag`, and `zratio_diag` are attached only when the run that
produced them happened: the first two by sampler choice, the third when the
hierarchical graph prior ran with its trust gauge enabled. Each is `NULL`
otherwise.

### Internal fields

Three fields are not part of the user-facing object and are documented here
because they explain behaviour elsewhere. `refit_step_sizes` and
`refit_inv_mass` hold each chain's final NUTS step size and diagonal metric, so
that a refit can start from them instead of adapting again; see
[Sensitivity and Refits](sensitivity-refit.qmd). `.bgm_spec` holds the
validated specification the sampler ran on, which is what makes a refit
possible at all.

## The lazy summary cache

Effective sample size, split-R-hat, and Monte Carlo standard error are
expensive to compute across every parameter, and many uses of a fit never need
them. So they are not computed when the fit is built. Instead `build_output_*`
creates `cache`, an environment holding the normalized chains and the metadata
needed to summarize them, with `summaries_computed` set to `FALSE`.

Every `posterior_summary_*` property is declared with an S7 getter that calls
`ensure_summaries()` and then reads the answer out of the cache.
`ensure_summaries()` returns immediately if `summaries_computed` is already
`TRUE`, and otherwise computes every summary the model has and sets the flag.
The work therefore happens exactly once, on whichever summary is asked for
first:

```r
f = bgm(Wenchuan[1:80, 1:4], iter = 200, warmup = 200, chains = 2)
f@cache$summaries_computed
#> [1] FALSE
invisible(f$posterior_summary_pairwise)
f@cache$summaries_computed
#> [1] TRUE
```

An environment is used rather than a list on purpose: environments have
reference semantics, so the getter can write the computed summaries back into
the object it was called on without the caller having to reassign anything.

`ensure_summaries()` also fixes the scale of what it reports, which matters for
reading the numbers correctly. See [Scales](#scales) below.

## The accessor contract

The object supports three ways in, and they do not all mean the same thing.

**`fit@property`** is S7 property access and reaches all 27 declared
properties, including the internal ones.

**`fit$name` and `fit[["name"]]`** go through the `$.bgms` and `[[.bgms`
methods. On an S7 object these forward to `S7::prop()`; on a legacy list they
intercept any name starting with `posterior_summary_`, run `ensure_summaries()`
first, and read the cache. That branch is what lets one body of downstream code
serve both object forms. Numeric indexing is refused with an explicit error
rather than silently returning a property by position:

```r
fit[[1]]
#> Error: numeric indexing is not supported for bgms objects
```

**`names(fit)`** returns `.field_names`, the names of the list that existed at
construction time, not the property list. For a typical ordinal fit with edge
selection that is 13 names, against 27 declared properties. The names that do
not appear are the ones the model did not populate, plus the internal fields.
This is deliberate: `names()` describes what this particular fit has, so a
conditional field shows up only when it is really there.

Reading a declared but unpopulated property returns `NULL` rather than an
error, so guard on the value, not on membership in `names(fit)`.

### Internal accessors

`R/fit_accessors.R` gives the package four readers that work on either object
form: `get_fit_cache()`, `get_fit_spec()`, `get_raw_samples()`, and
`get_posterior_mean(fit, field)`, which composes the field name from a suffix
so callers can ask for `"pairwise"` or `"pairwise_baseline"` uniformly. Package
code uses these rather than `$`; the `$` and `[[` methods themselves use
`S7::prop()` directly, since routing them back through the helpers would
recurse.

## Methods

`print()` gives one screen: whether edge selection was on and under which edge
prior, the model type with its dimensions, the case and variable counts, and
the total post-warmup iterations across chains. It reports the number of chains
that survived, which is the number kept in `raw_samples` and can be smaller
than the number requested.

`summary()` calls `ensure_summaries()` and returns a `summary.bgms` or
`summary.bgmCompare` object of the tables the model has, each with a print
method that shows the first six rows and points at
`summary(fit)$<component>` for the rest. Two of the printed notes are worth
knowing about. Blank cells in the pairwise and indicator tables are suppressed
`NA` values, which occur for edges that were never selected or whose draws are
constant, and the note says so; the tables themselves keep the `NA`. And in the
`bgmCompare` main-effect difference block, a leading `*` marks a threshold
difference that rests on the prior rather than the data, because some group has
no observations in that category or in the reference category. The counts
behind the mark are in `extract_arguments(fit)$category_support`.

`coef()` returns posterior means only, with no diagnostics, so it does not
trigger the cache. On a `bgmCompare` fit it returns both the raw
baseline-plus-contrast matrices and the per-group matrices obtained by applying
the projection.

## Scales {#scales}

The same quantity can appear on two scales in one object, and the object does
not relabel it for you. For a GGM fit, `raw_samples$pairwise` holds
off-diagonal **precision** elements and `raw_samples$main` holds the precision
diagonal, because that is what the sampler works in. The summarised views are
converted:

| Field | Scale |
|---|---|
| `raw_samples$pairwise` (GGM) | precision, $\theta_{ij}$ |
| `posterior_mean_pairwise` (GGM) | partial association, $\omega_{ij} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\theta_{ij}$ |
| `posterior_summary_pairwise` (GGM) | partial association |
| `raw_samples$main` (GGM) | precision diagonal |
| `posterior_mean_residual_variance` | residual variance, mean of $1/\theta_{jj}$ |
| `posterior_summary_quadratic` (GGM) | residual variance |
| `posterior_summary_quadratic` (mixed) | residual variance, $-1/(2\theta_{jj})$ from the negative association diagonal |

Two details follow from that table. The residual variance posterior mean
averages the per-draw reciprocals rather than inverting the averaged precision,
so it is the posterior mean of the residual variance and not a transform of the
posterior mean precision. And the conversion for the pairwise draws happens
inside `ensure_summaries()` before summarizing, so the mean, standard
deviation, and Monte Carlo standard error are all on the association scale
while zeros stay zeros, leaving the two-part structure of the selection
posterior intact.

An ordinal fit needs none of this: its draws are already on the association
scale.
